findings.title: Drain loop memoization couples correctness to object identity; state corruption on bundle reuse
findings.summary: The advanceAudit drain loop (src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts, lines 320-360) memoizes deriveAuditState results via WeakMap keyed on ArtifactBundle object identity. The design assumes bundle identity ALWAYS changes on every transition (line 235: `const finalizedBundle = { ...metadataBundle, ...}`). This is a BEHAVIORAL CONTRACT, not enforced by types. If any refactor reuses a bundle (via conditional path or executor mutation), the memoization cache silently returns STALE state for downstream obligations. This causes silent mis-decisions in the drain loop—the system computes wrong obligation sets, halts incorrectly, or skips valid work. The bug is invisible until that specific refactor or load pattern triggers bundle reuse. Removing memoization costs ~8-9x per-iteration deriveAuditState calls, but the current design trades performance for a latent correctness defect. This is adversarial-scale risk: structural code changes can silently introduce state corruption.

findings.title: File-lock timeout coupling creates deadlock window; concurrent holders clobber state.json
findings.summary: LockedJsonStore (src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, lines 14-15) derives acquisition timeout as STALE_LOCK_MS - 10_000ms to avoid stale-lock collisions. If a process holding the lock CRASHES between writing the lock file and releasing it, the lock sits for up to 30s. Multiple concurrent holders will timeout at 20s, assume the lock is stale, and ALL proceed simultaneously, clobbering each other's writes to state.json. The 10s safety margin is insufficient under high load or slow filesystems. On fast-iteration CI or large audit runs with many workers, concurrent timeouts become measurable. Result: corrupted state.json, lost work, silent data loss. The coupling is intentional but the failure mode is undetectable until it occurs.

findings.title: Provider auto-selection is one-way; no runtime detection or fallback on provider failure
findings.summary: resolveFreshSessionProviderName (src/shared/providers/providerFactory.ts, line 264) resolves provider ONCE at startup via static checks (PATH check, config inspection). It never re-evaluates fitness at runtime. A provider can resolve as available (line 135: `commandExists(opencodeCommand)`) but then fail at first dispatch: PATH entry is a directory, command requires unconfigured license, subprocess was killed, or network provider became unreachable. When dispatch fails, there is NO fallback to next provider—the whole batch fails. Design is "pick one provider and trust it" rather than "graceful degradation." On multi-hour audits, transient provider failures are measurable. System has no recovery path except manual retry.

findings.title: Token quota estimates never re-validated against actual usage; budget overruns cascade across waves
findings.summary: The quota scheduler (src/shared/quota/scheduler.ts) derives token budgets from estimateTokensFromBytes (file-size heuristics), but actual usage is recorded AFTER dispatch via response headers. If actual usage is 2x the estimate (cached request returns fewer tokens, LLM tokenization differs), the scheduler's NEXT wave has wrongly budgeted. The system does NOT re-plan in-flight work when it detects overage—it simply records it and continues. This cascades: wave 1 uses 2x budget → reported overages aren't reflected in wave 2 → wave 2 dispatches beyond capacity → 429/524 errors. Quota source is reactive, not predictive. Errors compound across multi-wave audits. Early over-estimation accumulates into late dispatch that exceeds all remaining quota, leaving work undone.

findings.title: External analyzer acquisition is consent-gated but not rollback-capable; persistent corpus corruption
findings.summary: External analyzer acquisition (src/audit/extractors/analyzers/acquisitionEngine.ts) gates all tool runs through admitSpawn with consent token. Once a tool runs, its output is PERSISTED into audit artifacts (graph edges, findings) immediately. If tool FAILS or produces corrupt data (Semgrep rule version incompatibility, false positives), system has NO ROLLBACK—findings are already baked in. Design is "acquire, run, persist" not "acquire, run, validate-then-persist." For non-default tools requiring explicit consent, operator-approved but buggy tool corrupts multi-hour audit run. Only recovery is manual state surgery or restart with tool excluded. Especially risky for ecosystem-native analyzers (clippy, eslint, rubocop, codeql) where version mismatches are common.

findings.title: Remediation dispatch merge tolerates contradictory outcomes; state machine reads corrupted state
findings.summary: Remediation dispatch (src/remediate/steps/dispatch.ts) dispatches work to parallel workers and merges results. Merge logic tolerates same node appearing in both success and failure (worker A succeeds, worker B fails for same file). Merge picks one arbitrarily or last-writer-wins. State machine (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts) reads merged state to decide transitions, potentially moving to closing believing all work done when actually items are in failed/ambiguous states. Test suite includes dispatch-merge-tolerance.test.ts, suggesting tolerance is INTENTIONAL, but tolerance has NO VALIDATION—contradictory merge can propagate. If two workers modify same file on filesystem with poor locking (network filesystem), both could report success, merge accepts both, final commit drops one set of changes silently.

findings.title: Git worktree cleanup assumes deterministic completion; lingering worktrees from crashed workers
findings.summary: Remediation dispatch creates isolated git worktrees for parallel worker safety. Worktree cleanup (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts) assumes when worker completes, cleanup runs. If worker CRASHES (OOM, uncaught exception, SIGKILL), worktree is left behind. Next remediate-code run against same repo encounters: (1) git errors (another process accessing repo); (2) stale filesystem state (worktree HEAD frozen at crashed worker's branch); (3) space exhaustion on repeated crashes. Session-start guard reaps idle worktrees >6 hours old, but that's slow band-aid. On fast-iteration CI, single crash blocks 6 hours of development. Design assumes cleanup is DETERMINISTIC (worker completes → cleanup runs), but real systems have asynchronous failures.

findings.title: MAX_DRAIN_STEPS is graceful-but-silent cap; progressive stall with no escalation signal
findings.summary: MAX_DRAIN_STEPS (advance.ts, line 48) is set to 64; loop halts when cap is reached, returning current state WITHOUT throwing or escalating. If obligation frontier exceeds 64 steps (dependency bug creates synthetic obligations), drain stops silently. Caller has no signal that work is incomplete. Next next-step call resumes and drains again, but human observer won't notice: if MAX_DRAIN_STEPS hit frequently, system appears to make slow progress, actually oscillating across frontier boundary on every step, never advancing. Return value has progress_made and progress_summary, but doesn't distinguish "we hit cap and stopped" from "ran out of work naturally." Obligation bug that keeps creating upstream ones could go undetected for weeks if cycle is shallow enough to exceed 64 steps repeatedly but deep enough to not trip hard error. Corroborated by P1 and P5 as structural risk.

findings.title: Two orchestrators claiming to be one logical core; separate state machines invite drift and duplication
findings.summary: Foundational principle (CLAUDE.md, project-philosophy.md): 'Auditing and remediating are two cases of ONE logical core.' Yet implementation has two separate orchestrators: src/audit/orchestrator/ (~30+ files, 3K+ LOC) and src/remediate/steps/ (~15+ files), each with distinct state machines, executor routers, obligation engines, validation logic. findings.summary: Staleness propagation (src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts) assumes once artifact is emitted by executor, content is IMMUTABLE—if executor runs again, produces NEW artifact with NEW hash or IDENTICAL content (same hash). This causes: (1) downstream obligation depending on artifact thinks it's fresh when actually stale; (2) false "no progress" signal when artifact changed but hash was cached constant.

findings.title: Artifact writes bypass LockedJsonStore atomicity, allowing concurrent state corruption
findings.summary: The LockedJsonStore contract (locked-json-store.test.ts line 1-55) enforces atomic read-validate-write with mutual exclusion. findings.title: Cascading worker failures have no circuit breaker; retry loops until timeout, draining quota
findings.summary: When remediation worker fails (subprocess crash, non-zero return), triage phase (src/remediate/phases/triage.ts) can retry or block. No circuit breaker—if underlying condition (compiler bug, code pattern) affects MULTIPLE items, each retried independently. Cascade could consume quota/walltime with no exponential backoff or global halt. Concurrency limit enforces PARALLELISM only, not total retries. Pathological case: 100 items fail due to same root cause (syntax error detected by compiler). Triage retries each (100 retries × 60s timeout = 100 minutes thrashing), draining quota with 0% success. Circuit breaker would halt after N consecutive failures from same executor/provider, allowing run to fail fast and request human intervention.

findings.title: OpenAI-compatible provider referencedFiles contract enforced at launch time, allowing dispatch-time violations
findings.summary: The openai-compatible provider's contract (types.ts line 36-51) states: 'A member that does not exist on disk is a to-be-created file...the worker writes it from scratch.' The launch method (openAiCompatibleProvider.ts line 227-235) validates all GRANTED files are inlinable, refusing with `grantedUninlinable` if any cannot be inlined. The contract gap: validation happens at provider.launch() time, but the referencedFiles list is constructed and passed at dispatch-build time. If a file is deleted, moved, or becomes unreadable between dispatch-build (packet creation) and provider.launch(), the contract violation is discovered too late—the packet was already dispatched as routable. Early validation at dispatch-build (when referencedFiles are assembled) would enforce the contract before sending the packet.

findings.title: Path containment check duplicated across five implementations
findings.summary: The same path-escape test (`relative().startsWith("..") || isAbsolute(rel)`) was reimplemented five times across different modules, creating a change-cost maintenance burden and a historical security gap where the fifth copy omitted the isAbsolute check.

affected_files.quoted_text: This check was reimplemented five times (audit dispatch paths, the TypeScript analyzer's include mapping, graph extraction, the openai-compatible provider's apply step, remediate's worktree seeding). Four spelled the same `rel.startsWith("..")||isAbsolute(rel)` pair by hand and the fifth omitted the `isAbsolute` half — which is the case that matters on win32, where `relative()` returns an ABSOLUTE path when the two sides sit on different drives and a `startsWith("...")` test therefore reads "contained". Five copies of a containment check is five chances for one to be subtly wrong, and this is the class where that is a security property, not a style preference.

findings.title: Structure executor writes multiple independent artifacts sequentially; fan-out loop opportunity
findings.summary: The `runStructureExecutor` (invoked by structure_executor) writes ~6 independent artifacts in a single call: `unit_manifest.json`, `surface_manifest.json`, `graph_bundle.json`, `critical_flows.json`, `risk_register.json`, and `git_history.json`. Each depends on `repo_manifest.json` and `file_disposition.json` (the upstream contract is identical), and each derives results independently of the others. Currently the executor runs these as a serial fold inside one runner. The opportunity: decompose structure_executor into 4-6 smaller deterministic runners that each produce one artifact family, schedulable as a parallel wave within a single `advanceAudit` call or across calls. The obligation frontier would expand (finer granularity), allowing faster convergence when one piece (e.g., graph) is stale but others are fresh. Trade-off: adds metadata/obligation-tracking overhead, but reduces re-stale cascades and walltime for partial-refresh scenarios. The dependency map calls this phase a whole, but the contract allows finer subdivision.

findings.summary: The AdmissionPool interface (admissionLoop.ts line 51-108) documents that `budget` is 'The MIN across the pool's windows' and serves as a fallback ceiling when `windowBudgets` is empty. findings.title: Artifact staleness DAG: sophisticated optimization but high cognitive overhead, questionable payoff
findings.summary: Audit maintains explicit staleness dependency map (src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts, artifactMetadata.ts) so upstream artifact changes mark downstream dependents stale. Logic tracks semantic hashes, metadata migration, dependency ordering, flow coverage baselines. Theoretically sound but creates complexity: artifact recomputation threads through staleness checks, tests mock artifact freshness, new artifacts require careful DAG insertion. Pragmatist question: does real-world payoff justify complexity? Most users probably don't care about maximal artifact reuse; simpler strategy (regenerate everything on resume, or use file modification time) would be less to maintain. Staleness system is OPTIMIZATION, not requirement. Cost of removing: ~8-9x deriveAuditState calls per iteration.

findings.title: External analyzer adapters duplicate schema mapping and normalization; template opportunity
findings.summary: Each external analyzer adapter (eslint.ts, semgrep.ts, rubocop.ts, clippy.ts, astGrep.ts, codeql.ts, npmAudit.ts) follows an identical pattern: (1) define interfaces for the tool's JSON schema; (2) implement a `mapSeverity()` function that maps tool-native severity → audit severity enum; (3) flatten/normalize items into a generic shape; (4) call `normalizeGenericExternalResults(toolName, items)`. The parsing logic varies (flat JSON vs NDJSON vs nested), but the flow is always the same. Opportunity: introduce a configurable adapter template that takes tool name, JSON schema, severity map, and item extraction logic, returning the normalizer function. New analyzers would be defined as config records rather than full implementations. Benefit: reduces code duplication (795 lines → ~400), easier to add new analyzers, consistent error handling. Drawback: abstraction overhead, harder to debug tool-specific edge cases. Current design favors flexibility per analyzer; templated design favors rapid addition of similar tools.

The executor is kept purely for backward compatibility with old serialized runs. Opportunity: (1) document the deprecation schedule; (2) if no external consumers depend on resuming v0.35.0 runs, remove the executor and its obligation entirely, simplifying the PRIORITY list and state machine; (3) if compatibility is needed, migrate old runs at load-time rather than keeping the executor in the active set. Benefit: simpler state machine (one fewer obligation), clearer obligation frontier. Drawback: backward-incompatible if a user has a paused audit from an earlier version and tries to resume. findings.title: Charter extraction, delta, and clarification are three sequential passes; consolidation opportunity
findings.summary: The charter layer runs three sequential passes: (1) charter_extraction_executor assembles charters from the consensus scaffold (Phase C.1); (2) charter_delta_executor independently mines deltas (Phase C.2, deliberately separate so it doesn't mark its own homework); (3) charter_clarification_executor runs the triangulation loop to resolve open questions (Phase D). Each is a separate obligation, separate executor, separate host-delegation round. While the independence of the delta-mining pass is architecturally sound (adversarial second-pass), the three passes could potentially be coordinated as a single umbrella obligation with internal phase gating (extract → delta → clarify) rather than three external obligation gates. Benefit: cleaner obligation frontier (fewer states before planning), simpler state machine. Drawback: less granular pause/resume control if one phase takes a long time. Current design optimizes for pause-ability at phase boundaries; consolidated design optimizes for simplicity.

findings.title: Design review contract and conceptual passes plus second-order challenge are three independent loops; unified loop opportunity
findings.summary: The design review layer runs three distinct loops: (1) design_review_contract (audit-findings contract assessment); (2) design_review_conceptual (conceptual design critique); (3) systemic_challenge_executor (second-order adversary, loop-until-dry). Each is scheduled as a separate obligation and invokes the host-delegation dispatch independently. All three are ADVISORY FINDINGS (leads, not verdicts) and all three consume host quota via the dispatch broker. The current design allows each to run independently and potentially in different dispatch rounds. Opportunity: unify all three as a single "design_review_unified" obligation that internally orchestrates contract → conceptual → challenge with consistent loop-until-dry termination (all three converge together rather than individually). Benefit: single dispatch coordination, clearer resource budgeting, stronger convergence properties. Drawback: less independent scheduling flexibility, larger single dispatch packet. The comment on systemic_challenge says "loop-until-dry second-order adversary pass" but the loop itself is implicit in the obligation re-firing; explicit loop orchestration at the unified level could be clearer.

findings.title: Metadata recomputation on every transition touches all artifacts; incremental update opportunity
findings.summary: Every `advanceAudit` call runs `computeArtifactMetadata(run.updated, bundle.artifact_metadata, [...artifacts_written])` to recompute metadata for the entire artifact set, even when only a small number of artifacts changed. The function computes hashes/revisions for all registered artifacts, then merges into the prior metadata map. The dependency-map then uses this metadata to compute staleness via content-hash comparison. Opportunity: implement incremental metadata updates that only recompute entries for the WRITTEN set plus their DOWNSTREAM dependents (transitively). Currently the function is conservative and recomputes all; an incremental version would narrow the recompute set. Benefit: sublinear metadata overhead as the artifact count grows. Drawback: more complex state machine (need to track downstreams at metadata-compute time), higher risk of metadata drift if incremental logic has a bug. Current design favors simplicity/correctness over performance — valid trade-off for a non-bottleneck operation, but worth reconsidering as audit complexity grows.

themes.title: State corruption & concurrency race conditions
themes.root_cause: Critical absence of atomic operations and proper synchronization on shared state. TOCTOU races on activeDispatch.json, memoization cache corruption from bundle object-identity assumptions, file-lock timeout deadlocks with concurrent writers all operating without sufficient mutual exclusion or atomic semantics. System assumes deterministic cleanup and single-writer behavior but encounters asynchronous failures, cache reuse, and concurrent access that silently corrupt persisted state.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Implement true atomic operations for all state mutations: replace non-atomic read-modify-write on JSON files with test-and-set or compare-and-swap patterns; add atomic flag checks before memoization reuse; enforce single writer via distributed lock with timeout escalation; use transactional write semantics (temp-then-rename) for all artifact updates.

themes.title: Missing error handling & resource cleanup
themes.root_cause: Pervasive pattern of awaiting long-running operations without try-catch blocks, missing timeouts on I/O operations, incomplete error handling for asynchronous cleanup sequences. Many functions documented to 'never reject' do not wrap calls in error handlers; script operations write files without catching exceptions; network operations lack timeouts. System silently leaks resources (temp directories, git worktrees, file handles, acquired locks) when upstream operations fail or hang, leaving orphaned state that blocks subsequent runs.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add comprehensive try-catch wrapping around all long-running operations; implement timeout parameters on all fetch/await/spawn operations (defaults: 30s for network, 5m for subprocess); add deterministic cleanup guards (defer queues, finally blocks); verify all promised cleanup patterns execute even on exception; add resource-leak detection to test suite to catch orphaned files/locks.

themes.title: Missing validation & type safety gaps
themes.root_cause: Schema contracts documented but not enforced at type level; validation logic applied selectively or incompletely; contradictory field combinations allowed by types but documented as mutually exclusive. Fields documented as required are typed optional; constraints (positive numbers, string-type values) documented but not validated at runtime; array iteration assumes array type without checking.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Elevate all documented constraints to type level via discriminated unions, refinement types, or branded types; add runtime validators that check every deserialized or loaded object against schema before use; replace optional fields with required + validation; consolidate contradictory constraint enforcement into single-sourced validator that blocks construction of invalid states; add validation gates before iteration/destructuring.

themes.title: Inadequate test coverage on critical paths
themes.root_cause: Large modules and complex orchestration logic without dedicated unit tests; test coverage concentrated on downstream consumers rather than foundational functions; functions exercised only indirectly through integration tests, leaving edge cases and error paths unverified. Many modules with 100+ lines of critical logic (quota scheduling, dispatch marshaling, orchestration) have zero direct test files.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Create dedicated unit test files for every module with >100 LOC or critical logic; focus tests on unit boundaries rather than integration paths; add edge-case coverage for empty inputs, boundary values, and error conditions; add property-based tests for deterministic functions (quota calculation, ordering, validation); integrate coverage reporting into CI to gate releases on minimum coverage thresholds.

themes.title: Code duplication & sync-by-convention maintainability burden
themes.root_cause: Same logic implemented identically in multiple locations (normalizeNewlines in 3 files, EWMA folding in 2, initRepo in 3, binding-window selection duplicated). Separate registries (PRIORITY array and EXECUTOR_REGISTRY) must stay in sync manually. Duplicated test setup patterns, duplicated command patterns, duplicated git wrappers. Every change to a duplicated function requires synchronized edits across all copies.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Extract all duplicated functions to shared modules and import everywhere; replace manual registry synchronization with generated registries (derive EXECUTOR_REGISTRY from PRIORITY array or vice versa); consolidate test setup helpers into shared test utilities; use DRY-enforcing patterns (sealed registries, factory functions) so new obligations/commands automatically register everywhere they're needed.

themes.title: Excessive function length & nested complexity
themes.root_cause: Core orchestration functions exceed 700+ lines (buildImplementDispatchStep 725L, mergeImplementResultsIntoState 903L, cmdNextStepBody 1225L, deriveAuditState 525L) with 4-6 levels of nesting. These functions combine multiple independent concerns (validation, dispatch, state mutation, quota tracking) into single units, making changes risky and dependencies hard to trace. Function length creates cognitive burden that invites bugs during modification.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Decompose each oversized function into single-responsibility helpers (one for validation, one for state mutation, one for dispatch sequencing); extract deeply nested conditionals into named predicate functions; introduce intermediate data structures to pass between stages; use guard clauses to flatten nesting; add tests to each helper independently to enforce loose coupling.

themes.title: Architectural structural issues: circular dependencies & orchestrator duplication
themes.root_cause: Three circular module dependencies (limits.ts ↔ scheduler.ts; remediate artifactStore.ts ↔ semanticProjection.ts; types.ts ↔ itemStatus.ts) create unnecessary coupling and initialization hazards. Two separate orchestrators (src/audit/orchestrator vs src/remediate/steps) implement identical workflow concepts via different mechanisms (obligation/PRIORITY vs state/phase), violating stated principle of 'one core, two draws'. Separate artifact management systems duplicate versioning logic. CLI exposes 27+ subcommands when conversation-first model calls for single entry point.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Break circular dependencies by extracting shared interface to third module or reorganizing so one module is purely consumer; unify orchestrators around single obligation engine with policy-driven draws (read vs write); consolidate artifact management into shared system with single versioning/staleness model; reduce CLI to single next-step entry point plus small user-facing set (status, cleanup); move internal commands to subagent dispatch only.

themes.title: Provider selection & external tool safety
themes.root_cause: Provider auto-selection happens once at startup via static checks, with no runtime re-evaluation or fallback if provider becomes unavailable mid-run. External analyzer tools (clippy, eslint, semgrep) are consent-gated but not rollback-capable: output is persisted immediately without validation, corrupting audit artifacts if tool fails or produces bad data. Quota estimates based on file-size heuristics are never re-validated against actual usage; overages cascade across waves with no in-flight re-planning.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Implement runtime provider health checks and fallback dispatch to next provider on first-use failure; add post-tool-execution validation gate before persisting analyzer results, with rollback option if validation fails; track actual quota usage against estimates and re-plan subsequent waves on overage detection; add circuit breaker pattern to disable flaky providers and escalate to host.

themes.title: Session config & contract versioning gaps
themes.root_cause: Session configuration persisted to disk uses no version marker. On multi-day audit runs interrupted for upgrade (v0.36.0 → v0.37.0), resumed remediate-code reads OLD session config against NEW schema, causing silent schema mismatches. Design review contract enforcement missing: test documents that contract MUST NOT inline review body, but orchestrator has no guard preventing regression where inline content is added.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add schema_version field to all persisted artifacts and session config; implement migration layer that detects version mismatches and applies transformations; add load-time validation that rejects incompatible versions with clear error message; inject contract-enforcement guards into nextStepCommand that validate design-review packets do not contain inline review body; guard should be executable on every build.

themes.title: Dispatch orchestration reliability: atomicity & merge contradictions
themes.root_cause: Remediation dispatch runs parallel waves but merge logic tolerates contradictory outcomes (same node succeeds in one worker, fails in another); state machine reads merged state to decide transitions without verifying contradiction-free invariant. Sequential artifact writes have no transaction semantics: if write(N) fails, writes 1..N-1 are persisted, leaving bundle inconsistent. MAX_DRAIN_STEPS cap halts work silently without escalating signal that frontier was exceeded.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add validation gate before state-machine transition to detect contradictory outcomes and escalate (block transition, replay wave, or escalate to host); implement all-or-nothing artifact writes via atomic temp-then-rename with rollback on partial failure; return MAX_DRAIN_STEPS cap as escalation to host instead of silent halt; log progress metrics to detect stalled work.

executive_summary: The audit identified 1925 findings across seven critical risk areas. State corruption from TOCTOU races and insufficient synchronization, pervasive missing error handling and resource leaks, widespread validation and type safety gaps, and inadequate test coverage of core orchestration logic present the highest-impact correctness and reliability risks. Architectural issues—duplicate orchestrators, circular dependencies, and code duplication maintained by convention—create high change cost and maintainability burden. Provider/dispatch reliability depends on runtime fallback mechanisms and validation gates that are partially or wholly absent.
top_risks: Silent state corruption on concurrent audit runs via TOCTOU races and deadlock windows; audits started on v0.36 and continued after upgrade to v0.37 face undetected schema mismatches with no migration path

Pervasive resource leaks on operation failure (unhandled exceptions, missing timeouts, incomplete cleanup) leave orphaned files/locks/worktrees blocking subsequent runs; session recovery requires manual intervention

Validation & type gaps allow invalid configurations to load and fail at runtime rather than load-time; missing checks on required fields, contradictory flag combinations, and array-iteration assumptions create silent data loss

Critical orchestration functions (700-1225 lines) with 4-6 levels of nesting create high change risk; modifications to state transition or dispatch logic risk cascading failures in interdependent concerns
Code duplication across 30+ instances (normalizeNewlines, EWMA folding, test setup, command patterns) maintained by convention rather than shared source guarantees drift and inconsistency
